utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in the courtroom and also to those assisting us just outside the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Good morning to you as well, Mr. Okun. I hope for the last time, because we hope to finish your testimony today, but -- so therefore I hope for the last time, but I have to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you have given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, are you ready to continue the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed. Cross-examined by Mr. Stewart [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Okun.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the close of yesterday I asked you about a quotation from Mr. Izetbegovic and I'll just remind you of it where he said "I would sacrifice peace for a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina but for that peace I would not sacrifice sovereignty." Would you agree that that can be ready paraphrased and accurately paraphrased as we, Mr. Izetbegovic and his associates, we want a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina, we would prefer to get it by peaceful means, but if we can't get it by peaceful means then we shall get it by other means. That's what he's saying, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't think so. I think he is saying that the country is sovereign. This is an understandable statement. Leaders, when countries become independent, are very proud of the fact. He's recognising the fact that in some cases violence has been practised against his government. That's the reality. The violence did not begin from the government. It was being -- the government was under attack. So he was essentially saying that they will defend themselves. That's the way I would interpret it, Mr. Stewart. By the way, could I ask you when did he make this statement?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I -- 27th of February, 1992, was the date that I gave you yesterday. That's what I understand to be --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. So it was made, then, on the eve of the referendum, which was February 29th and March 1, 1992. I think it's a standard statement that a leader makes of a -- leader of a country, that is, that's about to become independent and sovereign. I read no malevolent motive into it. In any case, as I mentioned yesterday, he had no army, and everybody in Bosnia knew that. So it would have been exceedingly foolhardy for him to put the interpretation on it that you've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Okun, I should say that I gave you the date both yesterday and today of 27th of February, 1992, but my client, Mr. Krajisnik, tells me that it was February 1991. So I'm -- I'm going to defer to him on that and --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we ---

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And give it to you on the basis of February 1991 and give you an opportunity to adjust the comment you've just made?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the comment is the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- excuse me. Excuse me one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave evidence of discussions --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, you gave evidence - this was on Tuesday, it's at page -- for those that have the transcript, page 80 of the transcript - of discussions on the 16th of April, 1992, and you -- well, in light of what I said a moment ago, I should make sure it was 1992, shouldn't I. Yes, it was. I've got the right year this time. The -- 1992, discussing the parties -- still discussing the Cutileiro plan, the map of March 1992. The map had initially been accepted by the three sides. We should more correctly say a draft map. Then the Bosnian government - and we've been over that at the end of March 1992 - withdrawn its initial acceptance. This was on Dr. Karadzic's mind and he's making a claim again for the ethnically based entities to be inside Bosnia-Herzegovina and he says "we won't fight after the map is decided." This is one of your meetings on April the 16th, 1992. And you were asked -- and Ambassador, is Dr. Karadzic saying to you and Secretary Vance that once the Bosnian Serbs acquire the territory they want or agree with they'll stop fighting, and you said, "yes, that was the clear inference to be drawn from that statement, deciding the map means deciding who has what. So when he says we won't fight after the map is decided, that obviously has to mean we won't fight after the division of the land is decided," and that was shorthand for that term. Mr. Okun, I -- the question I have really is that -- in that exchange of question and answer during your evidence-in-chief, and it stopped there then, whether you have in mind or are suggesting that there's anything in the least bit surprising or unusual or objectionable about the position being taken by Dr. Karadzic at that point in that exchange.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I have the page citation for that, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, page 80 and 81 of --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, the page citation. I beg your pardon. You're -- of course you're talking about the diary entry. Yes, I'm sure I can -- well, fairly sure I can find it for you. It's -- I think the reference was given in the -- yes, 70 and 71 in your marking.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I need.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it. Thank you. Yes. The remarks that he made, and I should say "they made" because the diary journal indicates it was both Karadzic and Koljevic on page 71, that we won't fight after the map is decided. The question I was asked and to which you are referring now meant that once the Bosnian Serbs had achieved their military aims in conquering the territory they wanted, and one knew but that along with that went the ethnic cleansing, that they would have achieved quite a lot. Note also, please, Mr. Stewart, that the very next entry, the next line in the diary, they refer to the veto, the blocking mechanism. They want that also you see. So this was yet another variant, another restatement, another asseveration of their war aims. Not all of them, because they didn't repeat all six war aims at the same time, but this was a fair and understandable statement concerning their territorial ambitions. That was understood by the use of the word "map." "Map" is the shorthand word for the territories. Have I answered the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Okun. And you were -- you were asked then, it's a -- it's a separate point in your evidence, you were asked on Wednesday and the transcript reference to that is for those who have a transcript is page 8 and 9. You were asked about information that you had received on Tadeusz Mazowiecki, and you -- this was in relation to camps, particularly, camps, detention centres, and so on. You said -- you were asked, "was the information you received from these various sources consistent," and you said, "Yes it was entirely consistent, I may say." And then you were asked, Now did you and Secretary Vance have occasions to let the Bosnian Serb leadership, including Mr. Krajisnik, know that you were aware of widespread ethnic cleansing or ongoing ethnic cleansing?" Answer from you: "Yes, repeatedly." Question from Mr. Tieger: "What was their response, Ambassador? Was there any meaningful attempt to deny that cleansing had taken place or was ongoing?" And you said, "No, they didn't deny the typical. Indeed, the almost invariable response was to point out the genocide that had been practised against the Serbs in World War II and earlier periods or to point to crimes that were" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you're reading. Your speed is going up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for reminding me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The typical, indeed the almost invariable response was to point out the genocide that had been practised against the Serbs in World War II and earlier periods or to point to crimes that were allegedly being committed in -- at the present time, 1992 and 1993, 1991, whatever, mostly in 1992 and 1993 that were crimes against them. The -- the typical response that you describe there sounds like your description of Mr. Karadzic's response, and would you say that that response was generally coming from Dr. Karadzic in the terms that you describe there?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It normally came from Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Koljevic, because they talked more than Mr. Krajisnik. That is the case. When the three were together or when Dr. Karadzic was together with Mr. Krajisnik, the response was the same. In this connection, Mr. Stewart, I should also mention that in the constitution of the Republika Srpska, which was adopted by the Bosnian Assembly under Mr. -- excuse me, under Mr. Krajisnik's chairmanship in February 1992, on the eve of the referendum, the Bosnian Serb constitution itself said that the lands that were to be claimed by the Bosnian Serb republic, soi-disant, which they were creating, and I'm paraphrasing here, that the lands also would include those areas which had been Bosnian Serb areas but in which they had suffered a genocide in World War II and therefore in the minority in 1992. I'm paraphrasing, I repeat again. But you see that they implanted in their constitution that idea that the lands that they should have in 1992, lands which they felt were theirs by right, included lands where they were in a distinct minority. And the reason they gave for that was the genocide of World War II. I mention that to show that this was not some figment of their creativity. It was not just a debating point. It was something that the Bosnian Serb leadership deeply believed, that they had a right to this land, that somehow they could restore the status quo ante, except that the status quo ante mention the restoration of the status quo ante involved expelling, killing, murdering, intimidating the people that lived there in 1991, 1992, and 1993. I think that is important to bear in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we know that the -- the only occasions, the maximum number of occasions on which you could have included Mr. Krajisnik in any such statement on your part in relation to this matter were March 19 -- were March 1992, and September 18th and 19th, 1992, because those were the only occasions on which he was present at meetings. Throughout that period you had quite a number of meetings in 1992. Do you say that -- that you let the Bosnian Serb leadership present at those meetings know at every meeting that you were aware of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At every meeting? They certainly were aware of it whether it was mentioned or not, because it was in the newspapers every day. It was in the -- on the television every day. This was a very intense period. So it formed a background, a -- it was part of the background to the meetings. Whether one said explicitly or not upon shaking hands when you go into the room, you know, you ask that kind of a question, but it was very much in the air because it was happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say this was a very intense period, you're talking, are you, about the period from the second half of 1992 as an intense period?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say all of 1992 after March become quite intense when the conflict began. The fighting began in March on a small scale and it increased throughout the spring and summer and fall, and you will recall, of course, that the shelling of Sarajevo began in April and became very intense, and that increased. So I would characterise 1992, after March, particularly after April, as all an intense period. I wouldn't put a number on the intensity scale. There's no Richter Scale for this sort of thing, but it was all pretty intense. That's why the London conference was called in August, precisely because the -- as you mentioned yesterday correctly, the effort of Lord Carrington was running into the sands and the situation on the ground was worsening. It was becoming more intense, and that's why the British government called the conference in August 1992 and why the international conference was established immediately thereafter in September 1992, in order to give an impulse, it was felt, in order to give an impulse to the negotiating to end this conflict which had become more intense in the previous months. Do I make myself clear?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Okun. And on Wednesday as well, and this is at page 10 of the transcript, you were asked by Mr. Tieger, who on a number of occasions was careful to include Mr. Krajisnik expressly in his question, you were asked: "Did the members of the Bosnian Serb leadership, including Mr. Krajisnik, indicate to you and Secretary Vance and the other negotiators that the use of force would cease as soon as the Bosnian Serbs got what they wanted?" And your answer was "yes." And of course a few minutes ago we were looking at a particular occasion, the 16th of April, 1992, on which Dr. Karadzic was saying exactly that to you, as you reported. You -- you're not in a position to say, are you, that Mr. Krajisnik himself personally gave you that indication on any particular occasion, are you?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's not written down, then -- then I would not say -- I would not put words in his mouth, no. But when you're sitting with three gentlemen in front of you and one of them speaks and nobody objects, had there been an objection, I would have noted it. I would have noted it, there's no question about that. So the assumption was that this was a statement on behalf of -- of the leadership.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described an occasion on which Dr. Karadzic spoke to somebody apparently in Banja Luka on a cell phone in the course of a meeting. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It may seem a remember detailed question, Mr. Okun, but do you have any recollection of that cell phone, what it was like?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't use a cell phone myself. I'm not a technical expert. And since I don't own a cell phone, and I've never owned a cell phone, I'm afraid I couldn't tell you one from another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's -- it's -- it's -- it's just -- I'm -- I'm wondering, Mr. Okun, whether your recollection of using a cell phone is in fact firm, because some -- at that time a network of cell phones was not available in that country.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can find the meeting in the diary journal. I recall it as I mentioned to you. It was an evening meeting in Geneva at the Palais, Lord Owen and myself with Mr. Karadzic, I believe it's described in Lord Owen's memoirs, and I'm sure you can ask him about it again. It concerned, as I mentioned earlier, the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt just for -- in that country, did you mean to say in Switzerland, Mr. -- Or did you mean to say in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I meant to say in the former Yugoslavia, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Since the witness is answering the question in relation to a meeting in Geneva, and -- I would say it's more or less common knowledge that you can make a connection between a cell phone and a fixed telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's point one. And the second is that unless you say that in Switzerland that at that moment there was no network of mobile phones but that would need further investigation, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it would, Your Honour, and I must confess that I don't stand here in a position to put to anybody whether there was or wasn't such a cell phone network available in Switzerland at that time, so I shall have to leave that point, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- you've mentioned -- you've mentioned Lord Owen. Lord Owen has written a number of -- quite prolific writer in various ways. Are you talking about a book called "Balkan Odyssey"?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one book he's written. He's written other things. I've not written everything Lord Owen writes, I confess. What I meant to say to you, Mr. Stewart, was that if you ask Lord Owen I'm quite sure he will recall that conversation, and I think that he may have even described it in print. That's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was -- the reason I mentioned that particular book is that I would like to ask you now about just three or four passages from that particular book by Lord Owen, Balkan Odyssey. We've got some photocopies of the relevant pages, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour. We know that the practice is to expect that the page before and the page after would normally be produced. We haven't done that right now. I hope Your Honour will accept that as a practical course. We will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the context, Mr. -- you see, my colleagues are reading what would come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Delighted to see that. One should never leave home without it, Your Honour. We will, of course, produce whatever batch of copies are considered to be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, can we look at page 32 is the first reference. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I won't start with the very first paragraph which is a bit of history, really, of how it all came about, but at the -- towards the bottom of page 32, there's a paragraph beginning "The Netherlands." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "The Netherlands had held the EC Presidency from the outbreak of the war in July until December 1991, and in consequence of my visit to The Hague, I discovered that on 13th of July, 1991, when the Slovenian and Croatian declarations of independence were just 18 days old, the Dutch government had suggested to the other EC Member States that the option of agreed changes to some of the internal borders between the Yugoslav republics might be explored. The Presidency continues to feel that --" and then that's a -- the next -- this bits of quotation: "The Presidency continues to feel that it is necessary to reconcile the various principles of the Helsinki Final Act and the Charter of Paris which may apply to the situation in Yugoslavia. It considers it especially important that selective application of principles be avoided. The principle of self-determination, e.g. cannot exclusively apply to the existing republication are being deemed inapplicable to national minorities within those republics. The following should be seen as a very tentative attempt on the part of the Presidency at structuring our discussion on the future of Yugoslavia with a view to developing a common position which may serve as guidance for possible troika involvement in the Yugoslav negotiating process. One, we seem to agree that it is not possible for Yugoslavia to continue to exist with its present constitutional structure intact. The joint declaration of Brioni clearly states that a new situation has arisen in Yugoslavia. Two, it is equally --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel please slow down when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two, it is equally difficult to imagine that Yugoslavia could peacefully dissolve into six independent republics within their present borders. Both Serbia and Serbian elements in federal administration, not least the JNA, have made it plain that they will never tolerate the emergence of an independent Croatia with 11 per cent Serbs within its borders. Three, a loosely structured Yugoslavia consisting of six sovereign republics is not likely to assuage the Serbian concerns either. The higher the degree of sovereignty for Croatia, the greater the need for solid guarantees for the Serbian minority in Croatia. The looser the federal structure, the more difficult it will be to supply such guarantees. The foregoing -- four, the foregoing seems to point in the direction of a voluntary redrawing of internal borders as a possible solution. It is clear that this option would entail daunting problems. In the first place it is impossible to draw Yugoslavia's internal borders in such a way that no national minorities would remain. Many minorities reside in relatively small pockets or even in isolated villages. On the other hand, it cannot be denied that if the aim is to reduce the number of national minorities in every republic, better borders than the present ones could be devised." I think I won't, unless I'm particularly pressed to read the -- the next two paragraphs of the -- the cited passage, and then Lord Owen's text resumes in the middle of page 34 with the word "incomprehensibly". "Incomprehensibly, the proposal to redraw the republic's boundaries had been rejected by all 11 other EC countries. The first ground for rejection was that it would open a Pandora's box. But the Organisation of African Unity while against changes to the map of Africa is defending the boundaries of states already recognised by the UN. Secondly, it was considered out-of-date to draw state borders along ethnic lines. Thirdly, it was thought that republic boundaries could not be redrawn in view of the large numbers of separate pockets where there were ethnic minorities not geographically connected. It is --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, for the record did you read minority where it says majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Perhaps I did Your Honour, let me see. Yes, I did. I -- thank you very much, Your Honour; I did indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do that sentence: "Thirdly, it was thought that republic boundaries could not be redrawn in view of the large numbers of separate pockets where there were ethnic majorities not geographically connected. It is true that there could not have been a total accommodation of Serb demands. But to rule out any discussion or opportunity for compromise in order to head off war was an extraordinary decision. My view has always been that to have stuck unyieldingly to the internal boundaries of the six republics within the former Yugoslavia, namely Serbia, Croatia, Slovenia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Montenegro, and Macedonia, before there was any question of recognition of these republics as being the boundaries for independent states was a folly far greater than that of premature recognition itself." Mr. Okun, do you -- do you agree with that -- that last conclusion there of Lord Owen that to have stuck unyieldingly to the internal boundaries in those circumstances was a folly far greater than that of premature recognition?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lord Owen is a wise and experienced man. On this point I do not agree with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your difference of view between him -- is it on the relative folly of those matters or do you not regard the ruling out of any redrawing of the internal boundaries as a folly or error at all?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the arguments given after the words "The first ground for objection," the passage you read on page 34, I think those arguments, that it would open a Pandora's box, that ethnicity was no longer the issue, you couldn't withdraw them, the arguments that you've just read, I think those are compelling arguments. I think they made sense. I must say I was not involved in this at all. This was the summer of 1991, and as you know, Mr. -- Secretary Vance and I became involved in October 1991. So what I'm stating now is simply my opinion now based on this. I had no involvement. But I think that the effort to redraw the boundaries would have led to more fighting and that the EC and the CSCE were, on balance, correct in rejecting the thought that is being put forward here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we can go on to page 41. You've just got a few clips of photocopies, Mr. Okun. It's in the middle of page 41. Lord Owen writes: "Cosic, Izetbegovic, and Tudjman are nationalists, if nationalism is defined at simply the determination of a people to cultivate its own soul, to follow the customs bequeathed to it by its ancestors, to develop its traditions according to its own instincts." I'm afraid we've sliced off the footnote reference that tells us where that comes from, but that's not the critical point. But is their nationalism a more malignant force than this? Serbian and Croatian nationalism, as it developed in the latter half of the nineteenth century, carries with it an inherent tendency to cross over into racial and religious discrimination and to ignite passions that feed on violence. Bosnian Muslim nationalism has historically been more benign, but the party Izetbegovic leads, the SDA, became evermore intolerant under the pressures of war. Pausing there, do you agree with that, that Mr. Izetbegovic's party, the SDA, became evermore intolerant under the pressures of war?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't use the word intolerant. I think they became more aware -- I would say they became more aware of their Muslim heritage. And the reason for that, Mr. Stewart, was they were being expelled by their neighbours. They were being killed by their neighbours simply on the basis of their ethnicity as Muslims. Mixed marriages were common in the former Yugoslav Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that when you take a person who is a, let us say, a secularised Muslim and suddenly harm that person, take an action against that person, when -- naturally he becomes more aware of what he is. If, for example, you looked at the most secular Jew in Germany in 1933, 1934, somebody who may have even become a deracinated Jew, and all of a sudden the Gestapo comes around and kicks him out of his apartment, denies him a job, beats him up because he is a Jew, well, naturally the man is going to become more aware of his Jewish-ness, as happened in Nazi Germany. So I think it's a fair statement to say that people under attack, under an unprecedented attack because of their religion, feel the religion more even if they had not felt it deeply previously. I think that's a normal reaction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The passage continues: "It was a reflection of Izetbegovic's pre-war view that the state was a means to an end, not an end in itself, that he opposed the break-up of Yugoslavia, was reluctant to press for an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina and was against recognition being granted to Croatia and Slovenia. Once nationalism had found independent expression in Croatia and Slovenia, he felt he had to establish Bosnia's independence from Serbia, Izetbegovic knew that this would lead to bloodshed. In his 'Islamic Declaration', he warned that the" - "Islamic Declaration" is a title of a work of his - "he warned that the Islamic Renaissance cannot be imagined without people prepared for enormous personal and material sacrifice." And would you agree with the proposition there as propounded by Lord Owen that Izetbegovic knew that this would lead to bloodshed?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the word "know" in that context has to be an overstatement. It is impossible to know things in advance. One may assume, one may believe, one may have a -- an almost certain belief that something will happen, but to know in advance, well, if that were the case, I'd go right out to the racetrack or go to Wall Street and become very rich. Nobody knows anything in advance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we then move on to --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it is true, Mr. Stewart, what Lord Owen writes here, that President Izetbegovic was reluctant to press for an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. He told Secretary Vance that to -- and me before the war. That is to say, he realised what the Serbs might do and where things might go. To that degree, as I've indicated earlier, as we all know, the situation in Bosnia became increasingly tense as independence of Croatia and Slovenia moved down the track. So of course he was aware of the delicacy of Bosnia and Herzegovina's position as the independence train for Slovenia and Croatia was moving down the track. Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever in the -- you've described the various remarks made, observations made from time to time in your meetings with the Bosnian Serbs about ethnic cleansing. In the course of 1992, did you ever -- you and Secretary Vance, say anything to Mr. Izetbegovic or his colleagues about their -- any suggested illegal activities on their part?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall some conversations about some activities, particularly at the beginning of the conflict in Sarajevo itself. Various acts by Muslim militants were carried out against the JNA in and -- in Sarajevo. I think if you checked a meeting with General Kukanjac in that period you'd see his mentioning it to us and our mentioning it to President Izetbegovic and Foreign Minister Silajdzic, Ganic. Those were our principal interlocutors. But the fact is, Mr. Stewart, that the ethnic cleansing was being carried out overwhelmingly by the Serb side. Therefore, it is not surprising that we mentioned it much more frequently, because it was happening much more frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we turn to page 63, and towards the top of page 63 there is a passage that begins -- do you see it, a paragraph that begins "In Sarajevo"? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, "In Sarajevo it became ever clearer that there were in fact two sieges of the city: one by the Bosnian Serb army, with shells, sniper fire and blockades, and the other by the Bosnian government army, with internal blockades and red tape bureaucracy which kept their own people from leaving. In a radio broadcast, the army, not the government, said that able-bodied men aged 18-65 years and women aged 18-60 years were forbidden to leave because they were needed for the city's defence, but their main reason was different. In the propaganda war, the Serbian siege aroused the sympathy of the world and for this they needed the elderly and the children to stay. It was their most emotive propaganda weapon for bringing the Americans in to fight the war, and they never waned it to be weakened." Is that passage consistent with what you know about the situation in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's broadly consistent, but Lord Owen here does not mention yet another fact which is relevant, and the additional fact is that, as we've discussed frequently here, the Bosnian Serb goal, openly stated, was to divide the city and to achieve a - if they could - a preponderance of the nationality, so that by asking the Muslim people to remain in the city, the Bosnian government also was opposing that goal because they didn't want to give the Bosnian Serbs the victory of dividing the city via the shell-fire. We've already discussed that point. So that's the additional gloss I would put on that, Mr. Stewart, but it is true that they also realised that there was value from the emotional point of view, to having the people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it's -- as far as Sarajevo is concerned, it was a proposal in the course of the Cutileiro discussions that Sarajevo might be under UN administration, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Proposals like that to put the city under some kind of UN or EC or CSCE or American or God knows what superior authority, they grew like mushrooms after the rain. They were very frequent, and they never -- they never went anywhere. There were many, many such proposals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one possible outcome eventually of a -- it didn't -- that proposal was not followed, of course, at that point, but one possible outcome of that UN administration would have been eventually some division of Sarajevo, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I doubt that. In any case, it was never a serious proposal, so I mean we cannot put, I think, pile hypothesis on top of hypothesis. I doubt it would have happened, but we're discussing two hypotheses that never saw the light of day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, you're familiar with the -- the European Union action plan which was formulated around the end of 1993 and early 1994.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The European Union Action Plan?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not particularly familiar with it but I have a general knowledge of it. I was not involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you know that that involved a -- Sarajevo being a separate district but there being a division of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Would Your Honour give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, we looked -- Mr. Okun, in the course of your evidence earlier, and there are two -- two differences, I don't think we need to dwell particularly on the content, but the references are last Wednesday, 23rd of June, at page 23, and then again at page 69. We looked at a map which has the Exhibit Number P211. That's the -- that's the large map showing the ethnic composition of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You -- I'm holding it up now just to remind you of which map we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we considered that. I'm going to show you another map.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, this -- this map which I physically collected from Mr. Krajisnik yesterday evening is not an easy one to produce lots of photocopies of in a useful form overnight. I hope Your Honour will be tolerant about that. It's a large coloured map. But of course we will, again, undertake to fill in any unnecessary gaps as far as proper material for the Tribunal and the Prosecution and everybody else is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stewart. As always, the Chamber tries to be tolerant, and certainly in this area. It's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber is succeeding this morning, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have a quick look at this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps, since we don't have any copies that we have a quick look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- That's entirely fair, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps in the meantime we could use the time to ask Madam Registrar to give an exhibit number to the excerpts of the book Balkan Odyssey. Madam Usher, could you -- we'd like to have a look at it for a second as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number for the excerpts from the book will be D22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And -- Your Honour, as -- since we are in a brief pause, as a minor housekeeping matter and in the same spirit with which Mr. Stewart has raised earlier housekeeping matters, I would like to note that we did not have an opportunity to see either the map or the excerpts from Balkan Odyssey, all of which I think should have been presented to us before Court. We would ask due to it that that be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps a five-minute glance at the map would be better. I do understand from Mr. Stewart that a map was provided to him only yesterday. I do remember that when we looked at the other map there was a comment saying that this was the wrong map. I remember that I then responded that this was the map presented to the witness, but now we see that another map is presented to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, can I say I -- I apologise for not having and/or taking the opportunity to show material to Mr. Tieger this morning. We do normally offer each other that courtesy and then we'll certainly try to continue to do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, I should say I don't want to dwell on -- on any detailed questions about this map, actually, it's just that I put it to you what it shows is that -- it shows the ethnic composition of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think it's the later stage on that map, somewhere in the small print is 1991, but what it does by comparison, would you agree, with the map that I referred to a moment ago, 211, the P211 that you referred to in your evidence, is it -- it shows a more detailed breakdown of the ethnic composition within the individual municipalities.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It purports to do that. This map was given to us, I have a copy of it in my personal file here. It was given to us at the conference by the Bosnian Serb delegation. I'm quite familiar with this map. When we asked them, How do you know -- what -- there's a lot of blue on the map. Well, that you see, that's the 65 per cent of Bosnia that belongs to us, and when we would ask, Well, how do you know that? There was never an answer given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you say -- take the word purported, Mr. Okun, but it does --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I use that word advisedly based on what I just said, Mr. Stewart. We asked them the question. Now, what one can do -- there are many maps. There's one there that you have alluded to earlier, this one that you've just given me. I preferred to use this -- this was the, ICFY map, this map, which I'm happy to provide to the Court as they wish, is a map produced by the -- because I think is the most complete. What it does is show some opstina by opstina, the entire country, including Bosnia-Hercegovina, of course --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. -- Mr. Okun, may I -- may I just interrupt you because I -- I very slightly swallowed a word that we -- didn't get picked up. You say -- you said it was a map produced by --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The US government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the 1991 census. What they did here was to take opstina by opstina and, based on the population, show those which had a majority and there they would colour it either deeply or less deeply on the colour based on the majority 50 to 85 per cent, 85 to a hundred. It's all explained. But where the opstina had no majority, they coloured it white. So you would have yellow for the ethnic Serbs, red for the Croats, green -- light green for the Muslims in Bosnia, and white where the opstinas had no majority, which I thought myself was quite a useful thing to do because it explained and was a clear visual indication of the most mixed areas, that is to say where no -- no nationality had majority. And there were various ways to do this. I mean, there are ways to show the ethnicity, the -- that map is a -- is an accurate one based on the census that -- that shows this, as I say, purports to because we see these -- you know, these snake-like lines running through each province, and unless one had gone to the land register, to the cadastre, if you did a Doomsday book of Bosnia in 1991, as William the conqueror did in England in 18 -- 1066 and 1067 and went through each parcel of land and said who owns what, you could come up with something like this. But to the best of my knowledge, nobody has ever done that kind of Doomsday book for the former Yugoslavia or Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is why I used the word "purported" to show. As I said earlier, as we all know, the Bosnian claim, and not just the Bosnian claim from Professor -- from President Milosevic on down, the claim was we Bosnian Serbs or we Serbs, if it was President Milosevic, we are 35 per cent of the population. In fact, there were 31, but, okay. We are 35, but we own 65 per cent of the land. That's repeatedly stated. And this map seeks to justify that claim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But would you agree at least so far as continuity of territory is concerned, that the -- I'll give you a moment?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry I'm wrapping this up. Should I pass this to you if you wish to see it or to the Court if they wish to see it? It is simply to indicate that there are various ways to indicate the ethnic composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it should go in somehow, Your Honour, because the witness has specifically dealt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's just what I discussed with my colleagues. So what I wanted to say to the parties is if none of the parties ask Mr. Okun to provide a copy in order to have it in evidence, then the Chamber would ask. So it's -- but priority to the parties, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it seems appropriate. Mr. Okun is a Prosecution witness who has produced this during the course of my cross-examination. I'm more than happy for, well, either of the Trial Chamber or the Prosecution. I think probably we'll defer to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think there is a consensus, Your Honour. We agree, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the Prosecution would -- we would invite Mr. Okun to provide us with a -- the original, and -- but then of course to make a copy and return the original to you after the parties have had an opportunity to inspect the original, and then it -- the Prosecution would tender that into evidence. Is that -- yes. Then, Mr. Okun, I'd like to ask you to leave the original at this moment, and we'll -- I think we do not need the original, Mr. Stewart, would we, or a copy would do?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm fairly sure. I think before it finally leaves court we'll get a chance to look at it Your Honour, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's put in the hands of Madam Registrar so that we could take care of copying it. And if the parties would inspect the original, Madam Registrar, would you give them an opportunity to look at the original, because I see there is some marking on it as well. Yes, but that seems -- from what I see just from a distance just your name on it, sir, Mr. Okun. Yes. Let's proceed this way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say a word?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I provided it to be of assistance to the Court, to Your Honours and to everyone room. I do not do this for the Prosecution or on a partisan basis. It is the map that Secretary Vance and I routinely referred to and most of the other negotiators. So I hope it's helpful. It's not a partisan issue. I hope that's understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do not know yet, Mr. Okun, whether the Prosecution or the Defence will find on the map includes -- that serve their position. It's -- it's in evidence that's what it is. At least it will be tendered into evidence. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Probably wise to put your name on it, Mr. Okun, since we've taken it from you. But that was -- that was foresight there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This -- Mr. Okun, so far as the map P211 was concerned, the one that you were referring to previously, the one that I'd just waved at you a few minutes ago, it's just in a hard form to my left there, you -- you would agree this much, would you, that it does -- that the presentation which is for its own purposes, the presentation of that map does at least have this relatively crude element which was -- which is that by colouring each municipality just as a single block, of course it does obscure, doesn't it, that within a municipality there may very well be divisions of territory where one bit of that municipality is predominantly one nationality and another is another nationality, so there may be -- you described them as snake-like, but there may be routes through by way of contiguity which are obscured by that presentation.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that's the case in any effort to put on paper the living reality. It did have the bars that indicated the actual percentage of the nationalities, the three communities in each -- in each opstina. That is to say there was -- the majority one would be green or blue, and then the minority ones in the map you held up were indicated. So there was no effort on that map to hide the reality. But, of course, as you cover the -- if you colour the entire opstina one colour, it -- it has a certain visual effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Okun.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Is there any need, Mr. Tieger, to ask further questions to Mr. Okun?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not sure how many questions the Court might have. I could proceed. I could also proceed a bit more efficiently if we took an early break and I organised my relatively few questions. I'm certainly prepared to proceed, but that might be one expedient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Then we'll have an early break. We'll resume at twenty minutes to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I take it that you're organised, so you could start your redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am prepared to begin my very brief redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Re-examined by Mr. Tieger:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, you were asked by Mr. Stewart about meetings in 1992 with the Bosnian Serb leadership at which Mr. Krajisnik was not present, and during your examination-in-chief, you stated that Karadzic would frequently mention his name, meaning Mr. Krajisnik's name, when he wasn't in the room. Did Dr. Karadzic indicate whether or not he would consult with Mr. Krajisnik about issues raised during the meetings at which he was not in attendance?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wouldn't be fair to say that he said every time on every point, "I will consult with Mr. Krajisnik," if Mr. Krajisnik was not in the room, or, "I will consult with Professor Koljevic," if Nikola Koljevic were not in the room, but it was clear that he would speak with the other leaders, and he would often say words to that effect such as, "I have to talk to the others," or, "I'll discuss this with my colleagues," that sort of phrase. So I think it was our correct inference that he would consult with the other leaders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, you also indicated during today's cross-examination that knowledge of ethnic cleansing was all part of the background of these discussions because it was happening and everybody knew it. I wanted to turn quickly to the meetings on September 19th and September 18th. First, on the 19th at R0163971. That's a meeting at 5.00 p.m. attended by Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Dr. Koljevic, Mr. Buha, and Misa Milosevic, and the second entry from that meeting is: "CRV: Detainees from camps. Need fix date good for you." And secondly, Ambassador, I would ask you to turn to page R0163962. That's a meeting of September 18th, one of two meetings that day attended by Mr. Krajisnik. This particular meeting was at 4.20 p.m. and included Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Dr. Koljevic, Mr. Buha, and Mr. Misa Milosevic. And also present was Madam Ogata on behalf of UNHCR. Ambassador, was the issue of ethnic cleansing not only in the background of those two meetings but in the forefront of those two meetings?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. That's why Mrs. Ogata was there. The meeting concerned the -- what to do about the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats who had been ethnically cleansed and who were in camps, being held in detention centres by the Bosnian Serbs or who were just wandering around the countryside. That was the issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Okun, Judge Canivell has one or more questions for you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, please, I would like to know the -- about this map you had lately shown to us, who provided you with this map?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, you mean the very last one that I gave to the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Yes, the last one we didn't know and you had produced --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was produced by the United States government mapping service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Yes. So you don't know what sources or what date it was handed or used by those services for making this map? It's -- normally you find that these sources are reliable enough to be taken without any difficulty.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in fact we know, Your Honour, precisely the data that were used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The data that were used were as the map so states, the 1981 census, the official Yugoslav census of 1981. And if you turn the map over, you will see the census figures on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's one of the reasons it was very useful to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the map, and it had the census figures for every opstina in the entire country, and it was therefore very, very useful for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There's no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi also has one or more questions for you. JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] I should like to ask you several questions in order to be able to understand your testimony better. And my first question is this: It has to do with what you said regarding the -- the moving the venue of the international conference to New York, and I think you said, and I'm quoting: "[In English] The conference moved to New York to be closer to the UN and to the decision-makers in Washington." [Interpretation] My question concerns the sentence you used, and I'm quoting: "[In English] The decision-makers in Washington." [Interpretation] What did you mean when you said "the decision-makers in Washington"?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation, Your Honour, was the following: The International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia was convened by the EC, the European Community, and the United Nations. Secretary Vance and I worked in our capacity for the UN. Lord Owen was the EC negotiator. So that the EC, for example, was fully informed of events that were happening in the conference because Lord Owen would routinely have his staff draft either every day or on an almost daily basis a report of what had gone on in the conference. You will understand that's important, because many of the sessions were closed, particularly the negotiating sessions. The UN was informed via our team. The absentee at the table was the United States. It only got the very small and inadequate reporting of the UN people, and it was felt that given the importance of the country and the interest in the situation that more American involvement would have been desirable, indeed both of the co-chairmen, Secretary Vance and Lord Owen, would have wished this to be the case, but it did not happen. So that when we returned to be at the United Nations, that was the principal reason for the returning to New York, to be at the United Nations, but in February of 1993. An ancillary reason which I mentioned in the answer which you've cited was to be closer to Washington also so that the Americans could be kept informed of what was happening at the conference, because Secretary Vance and Lord Owen felt, and indeed so did I, that the American government was inadequately informed about the developments at the conference. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] So you're in fact confirming my initial understanding of the matter, which is that from 1993, the United States played a role, which can be said to have been active, and if I can put it this way, replaced the role played by the European Community. So it was the United States' involvement which was emphasised after 1993. It was stepped up after 1993.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It would be incorrect to say that the United States replaced the EC. The United States never replaced the EC; rather, it became a more active observer. They appointed, for example, they being the new US administration, appointed an observer to the conference when it came back to New York. Reginald Bartholomew by name, a distinguished American diplomat, and Mr. Bartholomew, you will note from my diary journals, was present in Athens when the Bosnian Serbs, when Dr. Karadzic signed the Vance-Owen Plan. But it was never a question of replacing the EC. Rather, it was a case of a more active role as observer. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for giving me that clarification. I should now like to go on to another area, and that is the following, and I would like to focus, if I may, principally on the period starting from July 1991 to the 30th of December, 1992, that period. You were asked a number of questions concerning your meeting with Mr. Krajisnik, and you asserted that you met him in the month of September, that you had meetings on the 18th and 19th of September, 1992, in fact. Now, did you have occasion to meet him during that period of time? Would that be yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meetings were all indicated in the diary. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] So it was just the meetings in the course of those two days, that is to say on the 18th and 19th of September; is that right? That's the only time during that period?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The physical presence was on those days. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you very much. That's what I meant. And can you also confirm that during those two days you spoke in one way or another of the fact that there were detention centres? Did you touch upon the subject of detention centres? I would like to have the specifics, please. I would like to know whether you discussed genocide at any point, and ethnic cleansing or detention centres. So what, in fact, were the subjects discussed and expressly mentioned during those two-day meetings?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes, please go ahead. Take your time.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On September 18, 1992, in Geneva, we met for more than an hour with Mr. Krajisnik, Dr. Karadzic, Koljevic, Buha, and Misa Milosevic, and the entire discussion of more than one hour concerned the ethnic cleansing. That is on page R0163962 and R0163963 of the diary journal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt are for one second. I had the pages on my screen. I do not have then any more. Could they be restored.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I might just read, Your Honour, while it's coming. I'll read from -- I'm quoting the diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have it on our screen now, again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a meeting that Madame Ogata, who was the chairman of the humanitarian working group of the international conference, and, of course, simultaneously the head of the United Nations high commission on refugees which incidentally had been made as the legal agency for the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. For the first time a lead agency was secretaried by the Secretary-General to direct all of the work of the United Nations in the area, and it was precisely because of the ethnic cleansing that Secretary-General designated Mrs. Ogata as the lead agency. In any case, I now look and read the notes. Mrs. Ogata began by explaining, and I write "Statement to be signed." That statement was a statement by the parties, particularly the Bosnian Serbs, that was permitting the UNHCR to remove the displaced Muslims and Croats from the detention centres where they had been placed by the Bosnian Serbs as a result of the ethnic cleansing, of the killings. Next I note Koljevic -- JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting you, but just to clarify one point, to check it out. My question was precisely concerned with this: I understood that they were detention centres, and so with hindsight, these detention centres, did you mean to say ethnic cleansing, at the back of our mind?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The persons who were held, the civilians, the men, women, and children, were civilians. They were in detention centres because they had been ethnically cleansed from their areas. Yes, Your Honour. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] So the subject was broached, was it, explicitly?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was broached explicitly, yes, Your Honour. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] So my question is this, then: Did you receive any reaction from Mr. Krajisnik on that score?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reaction from the three Bosnian leaders was enunciated by Koljevic and Dr. Karadzic because they spoke English and we wanted to move the conversation along. And as you see on page R0163962, Koljevic's immediate reaction was, and I quote here: "Complains about lack of aid for the Serbs, especially in Sarajevo. Asks for the route." That is to say by what route would the ethnically cleansed Muslims and Croats be taken out of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You see, they were being taken out of the country. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. Now I'd like to move on to another area, but the subject does have to do with what we have just been discussing. You testified to the effect that you said to Dr. Karadzic that -- with respect to talking about genocide, his words led -- would lead to pre-emptive genocide as you put it, the term you used, pre-emptive genocide. Now, what was the reaction on Mr. Karadzic's part when you said that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a conversation between just the two of us before the war began, and he simply waved it off. I mean, he just shrugged it off. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] But you do assert that you said -- or, rather, that he said to you, and this was mentioned on the 2nd of December, 1991, and I quote: "[In English] War would be disastrous."

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He routinely made statements like that. At the same time, Your Honour, at the same time and in the same conversation, indeed only minutes later, he said, in that same conversation of December 2, 1991, that "if the Serb opstinas in Bosnia-Herzegovina were not joined to Yugoslavia, there would be war." Well, these anomalous, indeed contradictory statements by Dr. Karadzic were quite frequent. Here you have the man on the one hand saying "war would be disastrous" and two minutes later he says "there will be war." But that is Dr. Karadzic. That is the way he speaks. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. Now based on your own experience, did you feel that he was sincere?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I felt he was sincere when he said there would be war. I did not judge him to be sincere when he said war would be disastrous, unless he meant it would be disastrous for the Muslims and the Croats. That he also said. I mean, there are frequent references to that throughout the diary about how the Muslims, you know, are -- are going to end up badly, that sort of thing. That was quite common. I must say, Your Honour, excuse me for adding just this one sentence, but as I've said before and I would like to indicate because I think it's useful for the Court when you read Dr. Karadzic's statements, he is given to extravagant overstatement. One does extract from that the meaning, but he is given to these contradictory outbursts. And we knew how to judge them because, after all, we judged the actions. We have the proverb, actions speak louder than words, and we were judging these words against these actions. But when he said there would be war, there would be war if the Serb opstinas would not be joined to Yugoslavia. Well, then three months later there was fighting. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answers. I would like to ask you this. In your opinion, and you spoke about the decision taken by the Assembly of the Serb people in Bosnia, mentioning the six principle -- six principles, priority principles, the six basic principles, if I remember correctly. It was a decision taken on the 12th of May, 1992, in fact, by the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, we spoke at length about those six priority objectives, and my question to you is this: I would like to focus principally on the division of the city of Sarajevo. Do you consider that a demand of this kind was legitimate, to divide it up?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say no to that, Your Honour, on the basis that the city had never been divided, to the best of my knowledge, ever. It had lived -- the populous of the city had lived peacefully together, the Bosnian Muslim, the Bosnian Serb, and the small Bosnian Croat number, plus the number of people who declared themselves Yugoslavs. If you look at the ethnic census -- at the census for 1981, you will see in addition to the three nationalities those who declared themselves to be Yugoslavs in answer to the question "What's your nationality?" So I personally could not see any reason artificially to divide a city. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Very well. Now you also spoke about your personal experience, and you said that during the month of October 1992, you were in Sarajevo yourself.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I gave the exact time, Your Honour, but during that period we visited Sarajevo, yes, I -- it may or may not October or September or, but in that period we made a few visits to Sarajevo, yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. Now, if I understand it correctly, at that point in time the city of Sarajevo was under siege; is that right.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Now, how were you able to enter Sarajevo and reach it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went either by car or flew. One was able at that period to fly in and out of Sarajevo in UNHCR aircraft. You see, in June of 1992, the Bosnian Serb army turned over the Sarajevo airport to the United Nations peacekeepers so that humanitarian flights of food and personnel could go in and out, but only on UNHCR chartered aircraft. So we flew on those aircraft. We also drove, I recall, on at least one occasion from Split through the -- through Bosnia to -- to Sarajevo. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. And you also said that you observed that the city had been bombed by between 3 and 5.000 shells per day.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not personally observe or count 3 to 5.000, Your Honour. That was the number that we -- JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Precisely. So where did you get those figures from and that information from?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I indicated in my previous testimony, the figures were provided by UNPROFOR, the UN military observers who were present in Sarajevo. They -- JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And you yourself, did you yourself -- were you yourself informed about the number? Did anybody tell you personally or was it generally stated in the media, for example, or by -- or by other information means? So was this first-hand knowledge?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, depends how you define first-hand. It was first-hand United Nations knowledge. The figures came from UNPROFOR military observers who reported them officially to the conference on Yugoslavia. They were not -- they were not figures from the journalistic press. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And you also stated that the city was inhabited by a mixed population, mixed ethnicity. The Serbs lived in buildings alongside other ethnic groups, so the shells were attacking whom? What were the targets? The forces that were holding the siege and launching the attacks on the city, they weren't concerned whether the targets were Serbs or others, whether they would be hitting one or the other.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the city of Sarajevo is a city of hundreds of thousands of people. Some of them lived, as in any large city, intimately in the same building. There were, of course, again, as in any other large city, certain sections of the city that were known to be by and large inhabited by one or the other. If, for example, one looked at New York City with its 7 or 8 million people and you asked the question where do African Americans live? The answer is they live all over New York City. If you also ask the question is there one section that is heavily African American, the answer is, yes, Harlem - a good Dutch name, I note in passing - is well known as the section that is 90 per cent African American. I think that's common in large cities that certain sections are occupied while the overall city is mixed. So there was no segregation, but at the same time Alipasino Polje, for example, an example that Dr. Karadzic used to frequently cite, he would say, "Let the Muslims have Alipasino Polje." Well, I'm hardly an expert on the intimate living arrangements of the Serbs and the Croats in every district, every arrondissement, every borough of Sarajevo, but to answer your specific question, the shelling was designed to -- fundamentally designed to separate the peoples from these areas that each one occupied, as I've indicated, but there's no question that the shelling, that large number of shells falling on the city was bound to hurt, bound to affect the Serb populous as well. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And this brings me to my last question. It has to do with what you said when you spoke about the retreat of the SDA, the SDA party, from signing -- what you were saying was that the president of the SDA party, after having signed the accords in March 1992, went back on that and withdrew his signature, in fact.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And that it was at that point in time -- you said up until then, that's what you said and I'm quoting you: "[In English] The Serbs were open to negotiate a peaceful settlement."

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could you repeat that, Your Honour? JUDGE EL MAHDI: Yes. "The Serbs were open to negotiate a peaceful settlement."

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall saying that, but if the record so indicates, fine. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes, but your opinion. That was an observation on your part. I might have misunderstood you, of course. But do you now assert that up until March 1992, the Serbs of Bosnia were open to negotiations and that one the SDA party withdrew its involvement in the process that the events took a different direction.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The withdrawal of the signature did not lead events to go into a different direction because the negotiations continued, at least until May or June. To use Mr. Stewart's accurate word, they were a continuum, and they ended up unsuccessfully. But the events at the end of March were a stage in the negotiations, no question of that. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes, but if one can put it this way, one can say that it was a turning date, a turning point, a fundamental point, in fact, a determining factor.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that would be an overstatement, with all due respect, Your Honour. I think it's an overstatement to call it a turning point, because it was an ongoing negotiation. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Maybe I wasn't making myself clear enough. What I'm saying is this: I gained the impression that I had understood you to say that the Serbs were ready to negotiate up until the end of March 1992.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were negotiating. All of the parties were negotiating. Whether the Serbs were negotiating in good faith or bad faith is not for me to say because I did not participate. My point, Your Honour, in seeking to answer the question is simply to indicate that while this was an important moment, the withdrawal of the signature, it did not end the negotiations because the negotiations continued. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] That's another matter. I'm talking about the attitude, if I can put it that way, of going to war and resorting to arms. So they were continuing to negotiate peace, but they were in fact resorting to weapons.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs? JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the -- they -- they were resorting to arms. We had seen the barricades go up in Sarajevo. We had accurate and correct information from the EC monitors about the ethnic cleansing. So it was a two-stage, two-track process. Yes, Your Honour, you're correct. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. Yes, thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, I've got a few questions for you as well. But I also need to be organised, just as Mr. Tieger. I'll mainly ask for some clarifications and whether I understood you well. You have talked about the claim of consensus in decision-making, referring to the meeting of the 6th of January, 1993. I -- did I understand you well that it's your position that asking for consensus decision-making where none of the national groups has a majority would finally paralyse the administration of that state? Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And therefore is not a sensible proposal at all.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You repeatedly used the expression "ethnic cleansing," and that seems to be a rather broad concept. I would like to hear from you what still falls within that concept and what you would consider not to be ethnic cleansing any more. If I may just suggest to you that on the one hand of the scale is just killing everyone of that ethnicity and on the other side of that scale is to convince them that it's better for them to leave. I'm not talking about the means, I'm just trying to understand the range of the concept. When you said, "We saw this ethnic cleansing," I understood what you saw on the ground was people being deported, people being detained. Where you would say or what -- would there be any non-violent way or a way without any threat of violence which would still be within your concept of ethnic cleansing, or would you require it to be violent, whether it's deportation, killing, mistreating, whatever, or a threat of violence, if you don't leave now, would there be any non-violent of a -- or a non-threatening with violence situation which you would include in your concept of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honor. I think I understand the question. I would say that the spectrum covering the phrase "ethnic cleansing" would necessarily involve at the minimum intimidation, deprival of livelihood, verbal threats and violence as you just indicated. The other end of the spectrum would, of course, be death. And during this period one observed, one heard from the hundreds of thousands of displaced Muslims of all of these modalities being employed against them. We, the negotiators, had had previous experience on a more limited scale of this, particularly as regards Serb behaviour in Eastern Slavonia, in Croatia, in 1991 where we were able to see it ourselves and to receive accurate reports of it. As I've indicated, we were in Vukovar the day it fell. We tried to get the Bosnian -- the -- excuse me, the JNA to release prisoners from the hospital. They took them out and killed them, that sort of thing. So we were not unaware of what happened before. But specifically with reference to Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were numerous reports from eyewitness accounts by observers, international observers, the press, others, of the range -- of the range of coercive activities employed by the Bosnian Serbs to do the ethnic cleansing. We also had the example of the request by the Bosnian Serb Assembly, in fact signed by Mr. Krajisnik, to the JNA to help the Bosnian Serbs - I have to put quotation marks around the word "help" - because the standard procedure for the ethnic cleansing was to first create trouble, start an action, "aktie" as they called it in German, to start some action, and then to call in the JNA ostensibly to divide the parties or to protect the local Serbs. That was the pretext. That was the standard pretext. The JNA has entered this opstina. The JNA has gone to Foca to Visegrad, to Zvornik "to protect the local Serbs." That was not the reality. That was not the truth. They were there to cooperate with the Serb irregulars in cleansing the Muslims or the Croats as the case might be. And that was the recurring pattern over and over again, and we were able to observe it. So to sum up, Your Honour, I think that there was always intimidation, force, violence, coercion involved in the matter. And the civilians, men, women, and children, who were in the detention centres, and bear in mind there were thousands upon thousands of them, were the result of this activity. They did not leave their homes voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's at least the way you used the expression, so that's for us a guidance to understand your testimony.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've told us what you had seen. You said it was clear to everyone during this these meetings that ethnic cleansing was on its way. It was -- it went on. And then you said we'd seen it. We also saw it in newspapers, on television. You have just drawn our attention to what happened, what you had seen in -- let me just say 1991, let me see what indication you gave about it, place, you said, I think, in Western Slavonia --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I mentioned Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
