utterances.text: Vukovar. Yes. Did you also see it in Bosnia-Herzegovina with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. -- Secretary Vance and Lord Owen reported back when they had been in Banja Luka after that visit that we have discussed already. They saw the results of the ethnic cleansing in and around Banja Luka during their visit in the autumn of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said you could also read it in the newspaper and see it on television, did you mean to include local newspapers and local television, or were you mainly referring to what I would say the outside world --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the outside world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd like to draw your attention to the maps. You said the map that the Defence provided didn't satisfy you. You knew about it not because it was from the Defence, but it does not give the information that would be suitable as a working basis. Is my understanding correct that this map is based on the 1991 census, the --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I see "1991," and I know that there was a census in 1991, but I do not read B/C/S, so therefore I -- then your map, you said, was based on the 1981 census.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if I understood you well. To that extent, they're not fully comparable, are they?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are 99 per cent identical. The difference between 1981 and 1991 was minimal, Your Honour. In addition to which the last official census was 1981. The 1991 census was never officially promulgated. I believe I stated that earlier. But there is no essential difference between the two maps. None of the parties ever claimed there was a difference between the maps, and the map that I believe Mr. Tieger introduced, the large one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that Mr. Stewart was waving around earlier, that he showed the Court, that map was also based on the 1991 census. The three maps are essentially identical in all serious -- in all aspects. They show a reality somewhat differently, as Mr. Stewart pointed out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The one gives more territorial details. The other one gives more information about the minorities, where the -- well, at least --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They present the data differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason that I say that I personally preferred to use the map that I have called the US government map, the one that I made available to the Court, was that in the opstinas where there was no majority, that map indicated it clearly by covering those opstinas white. Or perhaps I should be accurate -- more accurate in saying by not colouring it. So one could immediately see, as one does, as you look at the US map, which were the mixed or minority -- the opstinas where there was no majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you imagine that on the -- on your map, the United States government map, that an opstina would be white, whereas, for example, under the 1991 census figures that same opstina would be, well, majority Serb or --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there were a -- an opstina, and there were such opstinas, which, let us say, was 49/49, with one ethnicity or one religion, however you choose to describe it, having 49 per cent and the other having 49 per cent, a swing of 1 per cent is possible and probably did occur. It may have occurred. I don't know. In any case, it would be very rare. It would be very rare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would be exceptional. Then you talked about the number of shells counted by monitors in Sarajevo, and you mentioned a number. Were you informed also about was -- about whether there was an exchange of fire or whether the picture changed? Was this about autumn 1992 or would it include the period at the beginning of the fighting in Sarajevo? I think you said it started in April. Would that include the whole of the period or was it just a momentum, the number you gave? And were you also informed about shells flying the other way?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The UN observers, after they arrived in Sarajevo and they were in sufficient number to count the shells, they also counted the shells going back, the Muslim response fire, yes. So we had the count of the Muslim shelling as -- it wasn't shelling. The Muslim firing as well. I can give you the numbers if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were they, according to the -- first perhaps I draw your attention to a second element in my question. The number you gave, was that -- was that for the whole period up until -- October-on from April, or was it just April?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It covered the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean October.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It covered the period after the observers arrived in sufficient number in Sarajevo to do an accurate shell count, and we received these figures at the international conference in Geneva beginning in September 1992, because there was no conference before then in which we participated, and we left Geneva at the end of January 1993, as we've discussed, to return to New York. So it covered basically the period from the beginning of September through the end of January 1993. From September 1992 to -- through January 1993. And we did receive -- they did count the opposing fire from the Bosnian army, their firing also. So we got two figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were these figures of the fire of the opposing army, were they considerable figures as well or how would you qualify them?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can give you the figures if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you -- if you have them.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were 3 to 500 approximately. 3.000 to 5.000 on the Serb side, 300 to 500 from the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's 1 to 10.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1 to 10. And one should note that the calibre of the Serb guns was much heavier. This was artillery fire, and basically the Bosnian Serb army was responding with rifle fire and machine-gun fire. There was one period I should mention, Your Honour. There was one period when the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina gunfire equalled for a very brief period, it might even have surpassed for a few days that of the VRS, the Bosnian Serb army. That was in January 1993 when the Bosnian army mounted an offensive to try to recapture Mount Igman from the Bosnian Serb army. Mount Igman, as we know, is the dominant geographical feature, the highest point, and therefore a strategic, very strategic high ground to hold, and in January, the Muslims gathered their forces and made a serious effort to capture Mount Igman from General Mladic's forces. They failed to do so. They failed, and the Bosnian Serbs kept control, military control, of Mount Igman throughout the fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I do understand that your figures include, as you said, rifle fire and machine-gun fire, not only heavy weaponry?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The -- the figures do include that, yes. The figures we received from the UNPROFOR observers counted small-arms fire as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honour, but I was hoping for a clarification before the transcript moved farther. That's at 50: 23 through 25. The Ambassador said, "One should know that the calibre of the Serb guns was much heavier. This was artillery fire and basically the Bosnian Serb army was responding with rifle fire and machine-gun fire." I think from the context we should ask the Ambassador about the Bosnian Serb army. It's now at the top of the page, or the Bosnian Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it should be Bosnian Muslim army was responding. The Serbs had the artillery. The Muslims had the rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. Finally I'm seeking confirmation of my understanding of one -- of what I thought would be one of the main lines of your testimony at this Court. Did I understand you well that you said that even if the goals would be not necessarily politically incorrect, these political aims in the existing situation could not be achieved without the use of force when removing the non-Serbs both from areas where they were majority, if claimed by the Serbs, or where they were in a minority? Is that a proper understanding of your testimony? Because many questions have been put to you on whether goal three or aim five were as such legitimate or -- well, what -- not expressing necessarily a -- a wrong political ambition, but did I understand your testimony well that you said, in the present situation, to achieve these aims or goals would necessarily involve the use of force in removing the population, the non-Serb population from these areas?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, your understanding is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions. If the questions of the Bench have raised any issue, the parties would like to put additional questions on -- Mr. Tieger, you are on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One small matter of clarification, Your Honour, about which I don't think there's any dispute, and so I won't put it in the form of a question to the Ambassador. And it arose from questions by Judge El Mahdi about the meetings with Mr. Krajisnik in 1992. I believe the Ambassador said they're reflected in the diary. I think Judge El Mahdi I then indicated that his understanding that they involved only September 18th and September 19th. I think we addressed that issue yesterday and directed everyone's attention to a meeting on March 5th, 1992 as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's certainly correct. We did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- we did resolve that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A very short report on the 5th of March meeting. Mr. Stewart, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Further cross-examined by Mr. Stewart:

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you put on your earphones then you will hear also the kind requests of the interpreters about reading or speaking into the microphone. Very often I could do without as well, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, no, it's -- I -- I hadn't realised as I leaned over to the screen it would bring me out of contact, out of radio contact here. The -- Your Honour, it's at 36: 16 was the answer. Well, I better read the question. It's short passage. Judge El Mahdi, its -- it's easier if we have the piece of paper as well with us, Your Honour because otherwise it's not easy to understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's -- it relates, Mr. Okun, to the meeting in Geneva. There's a reference number R0163962, but it's -- it's the meeting of the 18th of September, the one at 4.20 in the afternoon that you record Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Koljevic, Buha, and Misa Milosevic. Do you have that, Mr. Okun? In fact it's a meeting that lasted about an hour and ten minutes with apparently -- with a break of half an hour in the middle that you record so it was about -- in substance it was about a 40-, 45-minute meeting, something like that. I think that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have it in front of you.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the next page you record a break so it's about a 45-minute meeting in substance. That's not my question, Mr. Okun, that's just to set the scene. Then in your evidence in response to Judge El Mahdi's question, did you receive any reaction from Mr. Krajisnik on that score? Answer: "The reaction from the three Bosnian leaders was enunciated by Koljevic and Dr. Karadzic because they spoke English and we wanted to move the conversation along." And as you see on that page, Koljevic's immediate reaction was, and I quote here: "Complains about lack of aid for the Serbs, especially in Sarajevo. Asks for the route." And then you say -- that's -- that's unquote from your note. And then you say in your evidence today: "That is to say by what route would the ethnically cleansed Muslims and Croats be taken out of Bosnia-Herzegovina? You see, they were being taken out of the country." Now, looking at your note again, Mr. Okun, and what you record Mr. Koljevic having said, "Complains about lack of aid for Serbs, especially in Sara," that's Sarajevo, "asks for route, Belgrade, Uzice, Gorazde to be extended: Foca, Trebinje." I'm looking at that again and just considering that route?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Belgrade, Uzice is in Serbia, but very near the border of Bosnia-Hercegovina. Gorazde is then, of course, a municipality inside Bosnia-Herzegovina as you're going south-west, I think really from pretty much south-west from Uzice you're going into --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: South-east of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: South-east of Sarajevo but if you're copying down from Gorazde you're going near enough south -- south-west. You're -- and then Foca and Trebinje is right down at the --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bottom of the page of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's apparent, isn't it, that that's a route for aid for Serbs, and it follows --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can explain that simply, Mr. Stewart, if you have the chance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have the chance, Mr. Okun.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thanks. The question arose how to get the Bosnian Muslims out. They were being held all over the west and the east as well. The Serbs offered to take them into Serbia. This was an offer. They said, well, you know, we'll accept them. You can bring them and -- into Serbia. And that was discussed more than once. You'll see this route discussed quite frequently. And the offer was never accepted. They were by and large evacuated to Croatia. Some -- some went to Serbia, yes. There were no -- there were camps or centres. I don't mean that in an invidious way. The refugees were taken out. In addition to that - your point, Mr. Stewart - when he talked about lack of aid for Serbs, that route also could have served for aid, but in fact, in fact, the aid for the Serbs in Sarajevo, bear in mind this is the point he's complaining, as you correctly read, "complains about lack of aid for Serbs," especially in Sarajevo, they were being helped by the humanitarian flights that I've already mentioned from the UNHCR. The airlift into Serbia -- excuse me. Sorry. The airlift into Sarajevo was designed for the populous of Sarajevo. That's the only way they got food. They got enough. There was no starvation. But the airlift into Sarajevo beginning in the summer of 1992 when UNPROFOR took control of the airport, when they were given control of the airport by the Bosnian Serb army was a very effective airlift. Indeed, it was the largest airlift since the Berlin airlift of 1948, according to the numbers. It was a very big operation. So the complaint that Dr. Koljevic, Nikola Koljevic, was making was, without putting too negative a gloss on it, really phoney, because the Serbs of Sarajevo were being aided and assisted by air, and Nikola Koljevic knew that as well as we did. This was again their standard tu quoque argument, you see. It's our people who are being abused. It's our people who are being hurt. With respect to the Bosnian Serb population along the Drina in these -- these areas, well, they were living adjacent to Serbia. So there was no problem in getting food or, I may say, ammunition across the Drina to help them. So this was yet another employ, essentially, on the part of the Bosnian Serb leadership to seek to evoke sympathy where it really was not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Okun, your evidence was -- after all, you were asked specifically about this point in your note where Mr. Koljevic was asked for the route, and your answer was that what he was talking about. I'm paraphrasing the first few words, but that is to say by what route -- your actual words are by what route would the ethnically cleansed Muslims and Croats I can taken out of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In other words, you're saying that note of what Mr. Koljevic was saying is that he was talking about the route by which ethnically cleansed Muslims and Croats should be taken out of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, whatever the other explanation that you've just given in your answer, I am still putting it to you that it's clear that what Mr. Koljevic was talking about as noted there was indeed an aid route, not necessarily into Sarajevo, of course, because Sarajevo isn't Foca, isn't Trebinje, but the route he's talking of -- first of all, two clues. First of all, he's asking for the route to be extended. He's not offering it. He's asking. And secondly, the route starts from Belgrade as expressed there, goes to Uzice, Gorazde, and he's asking for it to be extended down to Trebinje right in the very south of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's quite clear that there, that's what's talking about, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say as I mentioned earlier that that was part of what he meant, part of what we understood him to mean. He might even have had a preponderance of mentality in that direction. That is to say, that might have been his principal aim in stating that. But we all understood, and you can see by Madam Ogata's response, which you haven't read but I will read, Madam Ogata responds, "There are 68 air evacuation cases have been," in other words have already been evacuated from the Banja Luka area. You see, we were talking in general about the evacuation of people from Bosnia and Herzegovina, and you see how Madam Ogata responded. She didn't even respond directly to the point which you have just reverted. She discusses the question in general. And that's what I tried to do in my response a few moments ago, to point out that the overall situation was being discussed. And you know, we had these discussions quite frequently with the parties so that both they and we understood pretty well what they were driving at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Okun, yes, what Mrs. Ogata said next I didn't -- I didn't read out, but I suggest to you that -- it's your note, of course, but given the content of the note and given what you've discussed, I put it to you that what's becoming reasonably clear is that Mrs. Ogata explains and produces the statement of what's primarily her concern, what's primarily her item on the agenda and what's -- why she's at that meeting. After Mr. Koljevic has made his intervention, which as far as Mrs. Ogata is concerned would have slightly switched the discussion away from her agenda item, she switches it straight back again. But in between, Mr. Koljevic, if you like, the mini topic, I don't mean unimportant topic but in terms of the meeting. The mini-topic that Mr. Koljevic is dealing with, or the chapter heading is perhaps a better way for putting it. The chapter heading is aid for Serbs, and there are two elements about Sarajevo. You have made your comments about that, Mr. Okun. And then a second element of that is asking for the route, and I won't repeat what I've put to you but does --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. I agree. Mr. Stewart, they -- there was -- a route goes two ways. London to Southampton, Southampton to London.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think one must admit that, yes?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, we'll agree on that.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So one can be talking about the route and Nikola Koljevic could have said -- would -- did say and meant, I have been -- there is no argument about that. There's no dispute that in his mind he probably, for debating-point purposes, said get aid to the Serbs, ground assistance to the Serbs on the London to Southampton route. They also offered us, which I did not mention, here but it was a known fact, it was discussed frequently, you will see is it in other cases, they offered to take along the same route, they offered to accept Bosnian Muslims and the a few Croats into Serbia as they did indeed, as they did indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you saying that --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm simply --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- saying that the route went both ways and my previous answer gave you the London Southampton route. You are now pointing out the Southampton London route. It went both ways. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I point out something. It was one of your -- it was part of your question was that it was under the heading, aid for Serbs. I'm trying to find it. I do see the word aid for Serbs in the -- well, I'd say the first Koljevic line. Did I understand your question well that you were referring to that aid for Serbs as the heading of the whole of the observation of Mr. Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Your Honour. Perhaps I should clarify. When I was saying and I think Mr. Okun understood it that way but I mean it's obviously the Trial Chamber must understand what I'm putting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I acknowledge that. When I was saying, chapter heading, I was using that in a rather figurative sense. I wasn't saying that Mr. Okun's notes actually show Mr. Okun --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a mini -- it was a subsidiary part of a larger discussion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I think I used mini topic and then I just felt I should correct myself because the topic was important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, I didn't wish to imply by mini that it was some trivial manner, so I switched to chapter heading in the sense that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sometimes it's of some use not only to understand the answer, but also to understand what it is in answer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I would a hundred per cent agree with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But -- no, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Okun -- Mr. Okun, since the Judges have no further questions for you, this concludes your testimony in this Court. I'd like to thank you very much for having come to The Hague. You have been in this courtroom and other courtrooms for a considerable period of time. And you have answered questions of both parties and of the Bench. I'd like to thank you very much for that, and I would like to wish you a safe trip, I would say home again but looking at your agenda, it might never be certain that your next station will be home, but I wish you at least a good further trip whether it's home or not. Madam Usher, would you then please escort Mr. Okun out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that we have another early short break and then deal with procedural matters on from 12.30. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to discuss at least two procedural items and is open for whatever procedural matter will be on our table. Let's start with an easy one. We have -- we face some problems in the processing of the 92 bis statements and the transcripts tendered into evidence. I have sought the advice of the registrar, and I do understand that yesterday the parties have met with the registrar, because what we have at this moment is we have the statements attached to the motions in which their admission is sought, but finally they're not attributed to any numbers. That music sounds familiar to me. It's Windows again. Therefore, I did understand that the parties agreed that in order to have all the evidence well together, I know that when -- that is the prevailing programme in the world but is there anyway --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I had to do that in order to mute it. I'll try not do it again but I had to go through that step with it in order to mute it. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've done without the music for approximately my two and a half years at the Tribunal and it's now three times in two days, so if all your activity could be used to avoid further advertisements for --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yesterday's music was provided by some other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not addressing --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- other organisation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- any party in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We take the point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's -- so we have difficulties. We have all the evidence together. Therefore, the parties agreed, as far as I understand, that they will then provide the statements and the transcripts in an electronic form and that the electronic versions will then get the exhibit numbers. One of the reasons why we changed the system is also that when exhibits are attached to these statements or to these transcripts, then it's a bit odd not to have the numbers for the original document but have numbers for attached exhibits. As far as I understand, exhibits related to such statements and transcripts will get the same number but with an addition, A, B, C, et cetera. Is my understanding correct that the parties have no problem solving it this way so that we could soon, especially from the Prosecution, receive these exhibits in order to be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you're both.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We both feel so strongly about this issue but I'm going to defer to Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We hope their music's in harmony if they're going to stand up together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am not aware of any particular agreement. I am aware of an e-mail I received with a proposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I thought it would be wise to have everything dealt with at a practical level. So therefore the registrar met with the case manager as far as I understand from both Prosecution and I insisted also the Defence so that those who actually do the work could agree upon it, but of course I understood -- well, I'm not a specialist in chain of commands, but I did understand that the agreement by the case manager on practical matters would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My case manager has suggested that after getting the information that we get a chance to meet and discuss this and we have not had that opportunity yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say you're not there yet --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That is the position, Your Honour, because Ms. Cmeric didn't meet yesterday. That's not a complaint at all, but, yes, we need -- we need to do some more discussing on this, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. If you -- one of the main reasons is to have -- to suggest this to you is to have a full set of everything that's in evidence, whether it's in paper form or whether it's in electronic form but that it's there and that numbers are assigned to it. That's number one. And second is where both the Chamber and the other party is provided already with a paper copy as an attachment to the submission -- the application for admission into evidence under 92 bis, to prevent that we need another rule to produce the paper on which we print that out once again. That is what is the underlying thought that has led to this practical solution. But I will hear from the parties. Could we do it in this way, that if there is any opposition, any objection that I would hear from the party interested within three days, five days? Let's say a week, weekend, et cetera. Then the next issue is the proposal communally suggested by the parties not to sit until the end of July. The proposal is contained in the memorandum of the -- let me just -- the 10th of May, and it's called schedule concerning discussion between Prosecution and Defence in Prosecutor versus Krajisnik, and attached to it is a schedule for discussions on municipalities and experts. The Chamber has already indicated to the parties that we would follow the suggestion, at least to start following your suggestion under the close monitoring by the Chamber, and I would like to explain to the parties, before I give an opportunity to make further observations, why the Chamber is, on the one hand, not opposing again the suggestion but, on other hand, is very cautious to not lose any further time. Madam Usher, could you please put on the ELMO a calendar. What I've done is to put on paper how many days we could have been sitting in court, so I excluded UN holidays, and how many days we actually have been sitting in court, but I see that -- that's what this calendar shows us. You can also see that we actually were 46 days in court and that, as far as I can -- could you please zoom in a tiny little bit so that my eyes can still read it. That we could have been another 55 days in court. We couldn't say that we lost that time. We lost that time in court, but that time was used, I would say mainly to give a further opportunity to the Defence to further get on top of the case, and on the other hand, some of this time has been used for communications between Prosecution and Defence to see whether we could avoid some evidence to be heard in court and be replaced by compromised facts between the parties. That is also these efforts to reach compromises is very much at the basis of the submission, the joint submission by the parties to not -- not to sit in the month of July, and they have given a relatively detailed schedule of how they propose to continue these communications. They mainly deal with evidence on what happened in their municipalities rather than how the vertical lines would -- would have been. And also to see whether specific portions could be identified on which we would have to hear further evidence in relation to experts but what parts could be accepted, what issues could be accepted by both parties. I've prepared this calendar just to give an impression in colour on what the balance is now between sitting and not sitting, and I'd like to go back, first of all, to last December when the start of this case was discussed between the parties. It did not remain unnoticed that the Defence said that they would like to have an additional 70 days on from the 2nd of February not sitting in the spring in order to be sufficiently prepared. The Chamber has then made another proposal. I would say the 18 days to start with and this schedule has been adapted several times, mainly on the request of the Defence but in recent times also on the basis of joint suggestions made to the Chamber, joint suggestions by the parties made to the Chamber. I'd like to have a look at what until the summer recess this would mean to the trial. Madam Usher, could you please put number 2 on the ELMO. This would be the picture if we follow the suggestion of the parties, and we indicated already that in principle we are willing to follow it. At the same time, we see that the balance between time spent in court hearing evidence and the time spent out of court preparing and communications between the parties is -- is already different. In view of the fact that in December the Defence said that it would need 70 additional days if the schedule is followed, we, up till the recess, will have not been sitting for 80 days. I am aware that the 70 days the Defence had asked for in December were preparation days. I am also aware that it was very much stressed that days as such was not the same as certain periods. I think it's for that reason that it was the Defence that preferred to sit for the first 18 days and then have a more -- a more continuous period of a couple of weeks off to further prepare. I'm also aware that these 80 days were not exclusively -- are not exclusively -- were not exclusively to further prepare but used for negotiations or communications, however you call it. But the balance is such if we follow this suggestion, the Chamber has to consider whether the time saved from now on, because until now it has hardly resulted in any considerable reduction of court time, although there were some -- there was some expectations that this would be the case if we would allow the parties now to continue their communications, but the balance, as we see it now between green and red could not continue unless we would have results, results in time. The Chamber is not in a position to say that parties should agree on certain facts. It's not up to the Chamber to do that. The only thing the Chamber can do is to say, if the parties can agree on certain facts and if that would take some time and at the same time would save time in court and save witnesses travelling to The Hague, save -- well, a lot of other things are saved as well if we're not sitting in court, then this would be highly appreciated. If I look at the schedule for the discussions and what could be achieved until July, I am aware, and that's of course part of the next part of the schedule not yet on this calendar, that after the recess it would take us another eight to nine weeks to -- if you would work in the same speed as prior to the recess. It would take another eight or nine weeks to communicate, to discuss -- not us but the parties, to discuss the remaining municipalities and the remaining experts. That means that what is now asked for the month of July and what the parties intend to continue after the recess has to be successful, because otherwise a lot of time has been used. We are not using the courtroom. We are not sitting. We are not hearing any evidence, which would certainly cause a delay in concluding this case and concluding the presentation of Prosecution evidence and the start of the Defence case if it ever comes to that. So therefore, the Chamber wants to monitor closely whether the result of the communications between the parties would still justify us to not sit and not hear any evidence, because we can't do both, first spend 12 weeks on negotiations, communications, and then to say since they were not successful, now we have to spend another 14 weeks in court to do it. That is the reason why the Chamber insists so much on monitoring, because if we look what we had in mind in the beginning, that is case presentation 450 hours for the -- for the Prosecution, until now the time spent in hearing witnesses, so apart from the days, altogether was not much more than 175 hours, which means that we are not yet sufficiently on our way. On the other hand, the Chamber also has noted that the -- of course it was until now mainly the Prosecution, that they stayed well within the time limits indicated for the examination-in-chief. Altogether they saved up to 25 per cent of the time indicated, and then, of course, it depends on whether you take the first -- the first estimate or the second estimate, for example, if you would like to talk in percentages. It makes a difference whether you talk in respect of one or two witnesses of 25 hours or six hours. That's of course what you gain and highly depends on your starting point. But Prosecution is staying well within its limits. Defence is -- it's also highly appreciated that the Defence stays within approximately the 60 per cent rule, but the overall, I wouldn't say performance -- but the overall progress that we've made until now does not allow the Chamber to take any risk that further time is taken for preparations and for where we cannot have the expectation that it will then save time in court. I mean, a similar number of red days on the agenda in September, October, November, should also result in the reduction of the time spent in the presentation, especially of viva voce evidence of witnesses. It is only on this basis that the Chamber, with some hesitance but agreed to follow the suggestion of the parties, but after two weeks, that is on Friday the 9th of July, wants to be informed as to whether the expectations in terms of agreement on facts, compromise -- compromise on facts have turned out to be realistic. We then also would like to hear, as it was done recently by the parties, to see exactly what this will save us in time in court. How many witnesses do we not have to hear any more? How many experts -- how much time can be gained in hearing experts only on those points the parties have identified. It's only on this basis that the Chamber is willing to continue. And as always, if on the balance the time spent results in time gained, it will be easier for the Chamber to further follow your suggestions for the month of September and perhaps even October. I was speaking about days. It was assumed that on the basis of the 18 days start, that means a slow start of the case, we would have spent in court until the summer recess some 370 hours. It now turns out that we did spent in court approximately - I have not all the details of the witnesses available - some 135 hours. That's in general terms, and the Chamber wanted to explain not only to the parties but also to the public why we would not be sitting in the month of July to explain how there's a fair expectation that it would not cause any delays -- I'm not talking about further delays, but it would not any delays in concluding this case and delivering the judgement. It even gives some possibilities also for the Chamber to concentrate on other tasks this Chamber also has apart from hearing the Krajisnik case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, this is a -- a more or less a public explanation of why the Chamber, although hesitantly, followed the suggestion of the parties and why the Chamber wants a close monitoring of the developments. Is there anything the parties would like to submit in respect of what they suggested and what I said?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Nothing on behalf of the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, please. The -- at the beginning of what Your Honour has said just now, we were slightly dismayed because Your Honour referred to the proposal coming from the parties only as being in the terms of not sitting in July and made no mention of September. That was causing considerable consternation among the Defence team being fed into me from both sides but I didn't need it to be fed into me from both sides because I had that consternation myself. However, the better news is that it has become clear as Your Honour has proceeded that that was only a shorthand expression because Your Honour has made it very clear that the proposal agreed by the parties for submission to the Trial Chamber does specifically involve a package, if I may put it that way, of not sitting in July and then discounting, as Your Honour has clearly agreed, should happen, discounting the three weeks' recess because that is needed as a recess, the -- that it would continue on into September. So, Your Honour, our consternation at the beginning point has faded considerably as far as that is concerned. So, Your Honour, we remain, as we have been for many weeks in formulating the proposal, we remain committed to constructively approaching this project, if we may call it that. We would therefore confine ourselves to two observations -- well, three, perhaps. One is the general one. Your Honour, we do and we always will reserve our position as to what we would then submit if the Trial Chamber or anybody else claims the view to view that this particular programme was not going to prove to be constructive, because at that point it would, of course, be completely open to the Defence to bring whatever motion, make whatever application it made in the circumstances then prevailing with a view to the trial proceeding in a way that ensured fairness to Mr. Krajisnik, fairness in terms of preparation time and so on, and then whatever views the Trial Chamber had expressed in the past could only ever be provisional because the Trial Chamber would have to naturally approach any such application in a judicial way on the basis of the facts and the submissions at that time. So we -- we do accept the spirit of it, and it is absolutely clear in principle that none of this can be binding and set in stone because at every point, at every application and every consideration will have to be judiciously assessed in the circumstances prevailing at the time. So that's number one. And that's if you like an important reservation but not meant other than constructively, Your Honour. It just is always there. It ties in with the second observation, of course, which is a message which Your Honour has indicated on a number of occasions has been clearly transmitted by the Defence to the Trial Chamber on some occasions, probably relatively few. But it's been transmitted publicly but it's been submitted in an open way among the Prosecution, Defence, and Trial Chamber with a view to -- to practical progress, which is that the Defence has always consistently rejected and does with respect continue to reject the notion that there must be a trade-off of time spent out of court and sometime saved. The fundamental point, Your Honour knows, is that there must be adequate preparation time for the parties, and in particular in the circumstances of this case, the Defence. So simply as a comment mere, that when Your Honour refers to the slow start of this case, we assure Your Honour that it didn't feel like a slow start to the Defence. It had rather the opposite feel to the Defence. In fact, I have never been involved in a case which was further from what felt like a slow start. So we do have our different perspectives here. Those 18 days were about as quick a start as any team of the size of this Defence team in a case of this size could realistically have faced and was at the absolute limit of what this team could physically, let alone mentally, cope with. But we did cope with it. So what may look like a slow start from some perspectives wasn't objectively a slow start, we suggest, but certainly, subjectively, it didn't feel remotely like it. So, Your Honour, with those reservations, the third observation is simply this, that Your Honour observes that correctly, that the Trial Chamber is not in a position, of course, to impose upon the parties any agreement as to anything. The Trial Chamber can offer strong exhortation and encouragement and support for us attempting to reach agreement, and we believe that we have between us an extensive discussions between the Prosecution and the Defence produced a framework, a way of approaching the matter, some understanding of the sort of areas which are likely to be fruitful for agreement, an indication, as Your Honour has indicated, as to where we would draw the line between -- likely to draw the line between the vertical elements of the case leading up through the chain of command, which are at the nub of the case here, where it's unrealistic to suppose that there's going to be significant agreement there, because that's at the heart of Mr. Krajisnik's defence. So we know that. But the -- but there's a very large number of matters in relation to municipalities which we do believe open the way to agreement which is, in the end, in everybody's interest. Mr. Krajisnik's interest is to have his -- a fair opportunity to present his defence. It's not in his interests to take any longer than is consistent with that but it is vitally important to him that it proceeds at a pace which is entirely consistent with his defence being adequately and properly presented. But it does mean this, Your Honour, that there is a very -- there is a very careful line to be observed here, or careful path to be trodden, which is that just as the Trial Chamber of course has acknowledged cannot bring pressure on the parties -- cannot insist that the parties agree, there is clearly an implicit risk of indirect or implicit pressure here. We have and we continue to say and assure the Tribunal that we will approach this project constructively, but it is very important that we're not approaching it in circumstances where we feel, and I'd use the metaphor, Your Honour, that the Trial Chamber is breathing down our necks on this, and that is simply a harmless metaphor, Your Honour, that if we don't agree enough, then we will be brought straight back into court where our position, frankly, Your Honour, is we do need more time to be on top of this case, and we would therefore make an application almost inevitably. We -- we can't predict completely, of course, what the circumstances will be in two weeks' time, three weeks' time, but we can form a pretty confident projection of where we might be in relation to being on top of this case in three, four, five weeks' time and so on. As we get further into the future then it becomes a bit murkier, as the future always does. But we -- of -- we are -- do remain uncomfortable, Your Honour, about a suggestion that if we -- if we don't achieve the saving which represents the investment, if we don't balance what we're doing, if we don't produce enough with one coloured days as opposed to another coloured days we will be brought back into court and we will have to proceed at the -- to us, relentless pace. Your Honour refers to 175 hours. We look at that. We actually suggest that's not at all bad considering the way in which this trial started and is actually -- reflects credit on both parties here for having achieved that. But, Your Honour, if we -- if we are in two or three weeks' time, if it's just -- you haven't agreed enough, you haven't produced enough saving, we do the calculation, it's 23 per cent short of this, it's not going to be balanced and if we are dragged back into court, this is not in the end going to achieve the efficient and effective running of this trial. That is our position. It's in the end, the efficient running of the trial, as everything else ultimately the -- a matter for assessment of the Trial Chamber. Fair and efficient is key to every trial, with fairness being absolutely the dominant -- predominant feature. So, Your Honour, that remains a concern. I hope that we -- we undertake conscientiously and will undertake in full the obligation to keep the Trial Chamber informed, and we do understand that the Trial Chamber will not impose such onerous obligations on us in relation to reporting that we have to take up -- take away too much time from the actual work on which we're reporting so that it simply makes the position worse, but with a fair balance on keeping the Trial Chamber conscientiously informed which the parties will do and a conscientious attempt to agree what we can reasonably agree, we do hope that there will not be too rigid an accounting approach to how much time is saved and so on and that sight will not be lost of the fact that quite independently of all those calculations this Defence needs more time. And if we were doing none of this, Your Honour, if we had not gone down this very fruitful route of exploring the possibilities and the framework for discussions, Your Honour knows and has known for a considerable time that the Defence's position has been that we must have more time built into that. And we have in effect deferred that while we have cooperated in producing this constructive framework, and we have every -- at the moment every week or further week, every couple of weeks of evidence that we deal with remains very difficult for us, and we need that time. So with those caveats, I don't want to resile at all from the essential constructive approach which the Defence is offering to this matter, but I do wish to make all those reservations on Mr. Krajisnik's behalf more than clear. Because at the end of a couple of weeks of evidence that we've heard, it takes us several days on the Defence side just to catch up with all the incidental aspects of this case. Maybe they're incidental, maybe they're more important than incidental. It takes us several days to catch up on that. Even if you leave aside such things as normal life, which occasionally comes into the equation, and I hope that Your Honours will keep all those observations in mind but will also accept our assurance that we wish to continue, and we have already invested plenty of time and energy into this matter, and we will approach this proposal constructively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. I make a few observations. First of all, that should be clear to the parties. The question is not a matter of bookkeeping but the question is how to come to a decision in this case as efficiently as possible providing the accused had a fair trial. That's -- a fair trial is absolutely at the top of our mind. But at the same time, this institution and this Chamber is responsible for how public funds are spent, so we can't just lose out of sight the efficiency. If I tell you at this moment and if you look at the calendar I gave, that after six months, the Prosecution has approximately spent on the presentation of its case 135, 140 hours, and if we granted 450 hours, that means that in this speed, we'd need another three times six month just for the presentation of the Prosecution case, and that's something that's just not a possibility. That would bring us two years where on the basis of the figures we gave the Chamber had the firm expectation that the presentation of the Prosecution case would be concluded in early 2005, very early. I'm not going into any details at this very moment. The second observation I'd like to make is that where I fully understand that the Defence says we are not fully prepared, we're not ready, so if finally the communications would not have the results the Chamber would like them to have, so therefore we keep all our options open, it should not be forgotten that if you communicate -- if there's communication between the parties in order to see whether they compromise on certain facts, that -- at least that's how the Chamber understands it. That's not eight hours a day negotiating but preparing a specific municipality, getting fully acquainted with the details of an expert report and then see whether you can agree or not. So therefore, the time given to further communicate is time which also is expected to be used for the preparation of the case. And it's in that context that I mentioned the 70 days mentioned at the beginning at a December meeting of last year by the Defence, the 70 days they would need in order to be appropriately prepared for the case, and I compared that with the 80 days we finally have not been sitting if the schedule continues until July. For the Chamber it's just a choice. Do we have sufficient reasons to accept the suggestions of the parties not to sit and to see whether a lot of matters we otherwise would have to decide can be dealt with by the parties themselves, or whether we say we have not sufficient confidence that this will bring such results that it is to be preferred above just sitting here and hearing the evidence. When I drafted the calendars, I hesitated if I would make it read until the 9th of July or the end of July. The fact that you find the full month of July coloured red means that the Chamber has confidence. The fact that you do not find the month of September also in full red could be understood as -- that the Chamber still is aware that its hesitations are not necessarily improper hesitations. I think I have made all the observations I would have to make? And further needs? Then is there any other --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, yes, yes. The answer is yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answers. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I will try to be as brief as I can. But, Your Honour, we -- we do not see that any projection leads to the simple arithmetic that we multiply the period taken so far to cover 135, 140 hours of the Prosecution case simply gets multiplied pro rata to produce 450 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I could be -- I could be very short on that, Mr. Stewart. Until now, I've heard the reservations. I haven't heard commitments like, if we do not -- if it seems not to work out, we will make sure that within so and so many days we will -- I mean, I heard reservations, and it was on the basis of these reservations that I made this projection. But if you say that it's not necessarily, as some people say, you never know what will happen in advance, you can't say what will happen in advance, of course that's true always well. I just am giving a picture that if we had gone at the same speed, that it would presumably take altogether two years for the Prosecution, and I don't want to have a great discussion on -- it's a picture. It's a projection, and I could -- I could give you five reasons why not to use it, and I could give you another five reasons why it's of some use. But it's -- I'd rather not make it subject of debate at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't wish to make it the subject of debate either. I simply wanted to make that record. There is no projection that leads to that conclusion, as far as we're concerned. But if it arises, we could -- then we could debate it, but not today. In relation to the 70 days mentioned by -- in December by the Defence, which Your Honour has mentioned more than once this morning, we'd simply like to observe it's -- really follows from everything we've said about this case. The whole problem is: The Defence didn't even know enough about the case at that time to make any seriously reliable projection. We were only doing our best at that point on the -- on the little -- relatively little we knew about the case. So we do suggest that looking backwards that that 70 days, that's really ancient history as far as our knowledge and grasp and ability to project the case is concerned. It's of no value with respect now as far as our assessment of the position is concerned. And the -- the third observation is just briefly that, yes, Your Honour is completely right. We, with respect, entirely accept that -- and this has been part of our discussion that we would in parallel or in tandem we would proceed with preparation. We would proceed with our schedule for agreement on municipalities and experts and that there would be considerable overlap. Naturally you can't say, well, that doesn't count as part of the preparation, that part of what we would have to prepare. But we would like to emphasise it's only part of what we have to prepare because after all that whole enormous area which is excluded from the ambit of any proposed agreement is itself part of the preparation, and, frankly, I wouldn't have minded cross-examining Ambassador Okun after I had had the chance to really have an idea what all these international negotiations and agreements were all about beyond the very limited grasp that we've been able to obtain so far. And we just don't want too many more witnesses to be examined by the Defence when we don't feel we have sufficient grasp. But Your Honour has that message and those are our observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That message was clearly received.

utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one remaining matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
